subject: SlopCodeBench: Our Latest Session on Maintainable AI Code
body:
Hey everyone,

This week's 🦄 ai that works session dove into "SlopCodeBench: The New Metrics for Maintainable AI Code." It was a really interesting one!

The full recording, code, and diagrams from the session are now available on GitHub:
https://github.com/hellovai/ai-that-works

We covered a lot, diving into the latest SlopCodeBench results and discussing how we can give AI agents better 'back pressure' on code quality. If you missed it, here's a quick rundown of the main points:

*   **The "Slop" Problem**: SlopCodeBench highlighted that LLMs often struggle with long-term code maintainability. As requirements evolve, they tend to accumulate "slop" instead of refactoring or redefining abstractions, which makes the code harder to manage over time.
*   **More Thinking Isn't Always Better**: Surprisingly, some models (like Opus 5.5) actually performed *better* on maintainability benchmarks at lower effort levels (e.g., Medium vs. X High). This suggests that sometimes, more "thinking" doesn't necessarily lead to cleaner, more maintainable code.
*   **Giving LLMs "Back Pressure"**: We showed how integrating maintainability metrics and guidelines directly into the compiler or the agent's feedback loop (using tools like BAML) can provide crucial "back pressure" to LLMs. This approach significantly improves code quality and reduces complexity, guiding them towards better design choices.

If there's one key takeaway from the session, it's this:
Ultimately, if we want to build truly robust AI-powered software, we need to give LLMs explicit "back pressure." This helps them prioritize long-term code maintainability and quality, guiding them to sometimes "disobey" immediate task completion in favor of better, more sustainable system design.

If you have any questions, just reply to this email or ask on Discord: https://www.boundaryml.com/discord. We read every message! Happy coding 🧑‍💻

Vaibhav & Dex
